role: US federal judge writing an opinion analyzing the law, weighing precedent, and explaining the reasoning that justifies the disposition of a Title VII, FLSA, or SS-disability case
target: the law as applied to the facts of this case; prior precedent; the litigants' arguments
inline_evidence_example: the phrase "Tackett v. Apfel, 180 F.3d 1094, 1097 (9th Cir. 1999); the decision of the ALJ may be reversed only if it is not supported by substantial evidence or if it is based on legal error" is an observation that evidences a 'binding-circuit-precedent / substantial-evidence-standard' norm without naming the norm; the phrase "Plaintiff asks that this Court decline to follow Hine for several reasons" followed by the court adhering to Hine evidences a 'horizontal stare decisis within district' norm; the phrase "these statutory provisions, however, do not force an aggrieved party to exhaust her administrative remedies. The language of the surrounding sections are voluntary in nature" is an observation that evidences a 'plain-text statutory construction' norm; the phrase "Rennie called these cases 'wrongly decided'" used as ground for distinguishing them evidences an 'intervening-authority supersedes prior holdings' norm
polarity_hint:
Judicial opinions are dominantly REASONING-MOVES rather than overt complaint or praise. The judge's voice is formal, third-person, declarative. The dense norm-bearing moves include: (i) statements of governing standard with citation ("To survive a 12(b)(6) motion, a complaint must set forth 'a claim to relief that is plausible on its face.' Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)." — evidences a precedent-following norm with a level-of-court signal — Supreme Court binding); (ii) applying a multi-step framework (the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework for disparate-treatment Title VII, the five-step sequential evaluation for SSI/SSDI, the FLSA exemption two-prong test) and noting which prong is in dispute; (iii) distinguishing precedent on facts ("unlike the plaintiff in X, Plaintiff here did not...") — evidences a distinguishing-on-the-facts norm; (iv) endorsing or rejecting one circuit's reasoning over another's ("the Court adopts the Sixth Circuit's reasoning in X as persuasive") — evidences an inter-circuit-persuasive-authority norm; (v) parsing statutory text (text → structure → purpose → legislative history → canon of construction such as expressio unius); (vi) deference doctrines and their limits (Skidmore deference, Chevron — noting that Chevron was overruled by Loper Bright in 2024 if post-2024); (vii) procedural posture moves (standard of review on summary judgment vs. motion to dismiss vs. substantial-evidence review of an ALJ; burden allocation; what evidence the court may consider); (viii) doctrinal qualifications ("the rule does not apply where...", "X is the exception to Y"); (ix) explicit reasoning about stare decisis, the law of the case, or comity. Overt complaint or praise is rare and almost always directed at a party's ARGUMENT ("Plaintiff's argument is without merit", "Defendant's reading misreads the statute") or at a lower tribunal's reasoning under appellate review ("the ALJ's analysis was deficient because..."). Most signals are signal_type observation (a declarative legal proposition the judge is asserting) or suggestion (where the judge tells a future court / the parties how the doctrine should be applied). Complaint applies to a misreading by a party or a deficient ALJ analysis; praise applies to a circuit's reasoning the court adopts.

DATASET-SPECIFIC OVERRIDES (these REPLACE the generic constraints where they conflict):

(a) The input is a JUDICIAL OPINION (often truncated to 18,000 chars). Aim for HIGH RECALL across the WHOLE opinion: 8-25 passages per opinion is typical for substantive merits opinions. Each passage should be a doctrinally-coherent unit (a standard-of-review paragraph, a step-of-the-framework paragraph, a distinguishing-precedent paragraph, etc.) not a sentence fragment. A standalone case citation with no surrounding reasoning is NOT a passage.

(b) ATTRIBUTION RULE — signals must capture THE JUDGE'S OWN reasoning, not the parties' arguments quoted in the opinion. When the opinion says "Plaintiff contends X" or "Defendant argues Y", that paraphrase of a party's position is NOT itself a signal — the signal is the judge's own move ACCEPTING, REJECTING, or QUALIFYING that argument. The clearest cue is the judicial voice: "the Court finds", "the Court concludes", "we hold", "we agree", "we disagree", "the ALJ properly", "the ALJ erred", "Plaintiff's argument fails because", "Defendant is correct", "Substantial evidence supports". Also acceptable are unattributed declarative statements of law ("A claim is time barred if...", "At step two, a claimant must make a threshold showing...") which ARE the judge speaking in the doctrinal-exposition register.

(c) signal_type ENUM IS STRICTLY {complaint, praise, observation, suggestion}. (i) Most legal-doctrine statements ("To survive a motion to dismiss, a complaint must...") are `observation` with polarity `neutral`. (ii) The judge rejecting a party's argument or finding an ALJ erred is `complaint` with polarity `negative` (the complaint is directed AT the rejected argument or the lower tribunal). (iii) The judge endorsing a circuit's reasoning, finding an ALJ analysis sufficient, or adopting persuasive authority is `praise` with polarity `positive`. (iv) Statements of how doctrine SHOULD apply in future / how a party SHOULD plead / what is REQUIRED to make out a claim ("a plaintiff must plead factual content allowing the court to draw the reasonable inference...") are `suggestion`. Use `suggestion` sparingly — it is for prescriptive doctrinal statements that direct future conduct, not for descriptive ones.

(d) CITATION-INSIDE-PASSAGE: case citations (e.g. "Iqbal, 556 U.S. at 678", "Williams v. Giant Food Inc., 370 F.3d 423, 428 (4th Cir. 2004)") are part of the legal-reasoning move and SHOULD be kept inside the signal_text when they are integral to the move (when the judge is invoking that case AS authority). They should NOT be a signal on their own. signal_text 10-200 char window includes the citation when natural.

(e) The level of the citing court relative to the citing court matters and is itself a norm. A quotation from the Supreme Court is binding everywhere; a quotation from the same circuit as the deciding court is binding; a quotation from a sister circuit is persuasive only. If the opinion explicitly notes this hierarchy ("binding", "persuasive", "sister-circuit", "the Supreme Court has held", "this Circuit has held", "we adopt the Sixth Circuit's reasoning"), the signal evidencing the 'precedent-hierarchy' norm should include that hierarchical marker in signal_text.

(f) Bare procedural recitations (case caption, list of pending motions, who filed what when, "the parties have consented to proceed before a magistrate judge") emit ZERO signals. Skip the case caption and the PROCEDURAL HISTORY section unless the judge is using procedural history to make a doctrinal move (e.g. invoking the law of the case, or noting waiver from failure to raise an argument). The DISCUSSION / ANALYSIS / CONCLUSION sections are where most signals live.

(g) PRESERVE the source text VERBATIM in passage_text and signal_text. Court opinions often contain artifacts of OCR / PDF conversion: stray newlines mid-sentence, line numbers, "FILED" stamps, footnote markers (e.g. ¹, ², or simple superscript-1), section symbols (§§), em dashes (—), curly quotes (“ ” ‘ ’), and occasional OCR errors ("Jd." for "Id.", "LEIDOS" all-caps, periods replaced with commas, "S" replaced with "$"). Copy character-for-character. Do not normalize, do not correct.

(h) When two or more discrete doctrinal moves appear in the same paragraph (e.g. the judge first states a standard of review, then applies it), emit each as its own signal inside the same passage. 3-8 signals per substantive passage is typical.
